title: ​Severn Lamb and the changing face of attraction transport
summary:
Known for its heritage trains and trackless road trams, Severn Lamb is expanding its electric vehicle portfolio to meet the wider mobility needs of visitor attractions.

The Warwickshire-based manufacturer has traditionally focused on guest transport, with tracked trains, trams and road trains used across theme parks, resorts and other destinations. It is now broadening its offer to include compact electric vehicles for behind-the-scenes operations, from maintenance and security to housekeeping and logistics.

As attractions become larger and more complex, operators need mobility solutions that support both the visitor experience and the day-to-day running of the site. Severn Lamb's expanded EV portfolio is designed to address both.

Blooloop speaks to Patrick Lamb, managing director of Severn Lamb, about the changing mobility needs of visitor attractions and the role of electric vehicles in supporting guest and back-of-house operations.

​Beyond the guest journey


Electric propulsion is not new to Severn Lamb, explains Lamb. “We have been developing battery-electric passenger transport solutions for many years. What has changed is the breadth of the requirements we are being asked to meet.”


Severn Lamb's customers increasingly need more than vehicles for transporting large groups of visitors. They also need smaller vehicles for accessible transport, staff movement, maintenance, security, landscaping and other site operations.

“Expanding our portfolio allows us to support that complete mobility picture, from compact passenger and utility vehicles through to higher-capacity shuttles, road trams and rail systems."

"It is a natural extension of what Severn Lamb has always done: understanding how people and equipment need to move around a destination and providing the most appropriate solution.”

​The invisible network behind the visitor experience


When discussing transport at visitor attractions, the focus tends to be on the highly visible elements: the entrance tram, the themed train circling a safari park or the scenic monorail. Behind these systems, however, is a continuous network of back-of-house logistics.

This behind-the-scenes movement of people, equipment, supplies and waste is vital to keeping a site running. Problems within this network can ultimately affect the guest experience.

"Visitors may never see most of the work taking place behind the scenes, but their experience depends upon it being carried out efficiently,” says Lamb.

“Maintenance teams need to respond quickly, catering and retail supplies must reach the right locations, waste has to be removed, landscapes and facilities must be maintained, and security staff need to move around the site effectively.

"At zoos, there may also be equipment and supplies required for animal care.”


An appropriate back-of-house fleet can therefore improve productivity while also helping a site remain clean, safe and welcoming.

“It is an essential part of the overall guest experience, even if it is rarely visible."

Traditionally, attractions relied on conventional vehicles to handle these tasks. However, a conventional van or larger utility vehicle driving through a tranquil botanical garden or near sensitive animal enclosures can break the immersion that theme parks and heritage attractions work to maintain.

"We are seeing growing interest from operators who want to replace conventional vehicles with something cleaner, quieter and better suited to the environment in which they are working," says Lamb.

"Many attractions operate across large or complex sites, but the majority of their daily journeys are relatively short and predictable. Staff may be transporting tools, supplies, waste or small groups of people throughout the day, often using vehicles that are larger than the task requires.”

Compact electric vehicles are well suited to this type of work.

"They are easy to manoeuvre, can be configured for different operational roles and can return to a central location for charging. Sustainability targets may begin the conversation, but efficiency, practicality and operating costs are increasingly important factors too."

​Expanding the electric fleet


Partnerships with WAEV Inc. and EVX Mobility support Severn Lamb's expanded EV offering.

Announced in June 2026, Severn Lamb's partnership with WAEV Inc. brings WAEV's Compact Mobility and Utility EV ranges into its portfolio. US-based WAEV offers light-duty electric vehicles supported by a network of dealers and service centres.

The partnership also gives Severn Lamb access to WAEV's dealer and service network.

The partnership with EVX Mobility adds passenger-focused electric vehicles to complement the WAEV utility and compact range, including the Solar Shuttle.

"The continued development of our electric vehicle offering marks an important step for Severn Lamb," says Lamb.

"By building on our partnership with EVX and introducing WAEV's Compact Mobility and Utility EV ranges, we are expanding the range of sustainable solutions available to our customers and strengthening our ability to support a wider variety of operational needs."


WAEV's product line offers durable utility electric vehicles built for demanding site operations. Models including the Bigfoot, GEM eL XD and Fusion Utility are designed for applications including maintenance, landscaping, logistics and site support.

"The greatest value is generally found in frequent, repeatable journeys where a conventional van or larger utility vehicle would be inefficient or intrusive," Patrick Lamb says.

"Utility EVs can transport tools, maintenance equipment, landscaping materials, deliveries and waste around a site. Compact passenger vehicles can support security patrols, staff movement, inspections and the transport of guests who require additional assistance."

For example, utility vehicles can be configured to carry maintenance equipment, landscaping materials and other bulky loads. They can also support catering, retail restocking and waste collection, particularly where staff and visitors share routes.

Their smaller footprint can be useful at attractions where staff and visitors share routes, reducing the physical presence of service vehicles.

"Different configurations allow operators to choose a vehicle suited to the task rather than adapting their operation around a standard vehicle," Lamb explains.

​Supporting the guest journey


Alongside its utility vehicles, Severn Lamb's expanded portfolio includes compact passenger vehicles for resorts, gardens, historic sites and campuses.

The portfolio includes the GEM e2, e4 and e6, the wheelchair-accessible GEM WAV, GEM Ambulance, ShuttlePro XL and Fusion Passenger. Applications include guest and VIP transport, staff journeys and security, while the GEM Ambulance is designed for medical response teams operating on busy sites.

Accessibility is another important factor to consider, with features including wheelchair ramps, flexible seating and space for mobility equipment.


"Accessibility increasingly needs to be considered from the beginning of a transport project rather than added later," says Lamb.

"Attractions serve guests with a wide range of mobility requirements, including wheelchair users, older visitors and people who may find it difficult to cover long distances.

“The wider fleet also needs to provide enough flexibility to support individual journeys as well as larger-group transport. Good accessible transport should feel like an integrated part of the visitor experience, not a separate or secondary service.”

For higher-capacity routes, Severn Lamb also offers the EVX-powered Solar Shuttle.

"The Solar Shuttle bridges the gap between compact passenger vehicles and our larger road tram and rail solutions. With configurations for approximately 11 to 24 passengers, it is suited to regular routes around attractions, resorts, gardens, campuses and heritage destinations.”

The Solar Shuttle features a solar-assisted roof, wheelchair access and fleet-management capabilities.

​Planning for real-world conditions


For visitor attraction operators, electrifying a fleet requires more than replacing petrol or diesel vehicles with electric equivalents. Operators need to understand how vehicles will be used day to day, from mileage and payload to terrain, operating hours, and seasonal demand.

Lamb says the process should start with the task, not the technology: "Operators need to understand actual daily mileage, payload, passenger numbers, gradients, road surfaces, operating hours and seasonal peaks.

“The vehicle must provide sufficient real-world range with an appropriate margin, while charging needs to fit naturally into the operating schedule. Payload and towing capacity should be assessed carefully, because an unsuitable vehicle will create inefficiency regardless of its power source."


Key considerations include the vehicle's duty cycle, terrain, climate and charging requirements. Attractions may also need to account for gradients, gravel or cobbled surfaces, weather conditions and charging requirements. Charging can be scheduled around operating patterns, whether overnight at a depot or during planned breaks.

Seasonal peaks are another important consideration. Designing a fleet around an average operating day can leave operators short of capacity when visitor numbers are highest.

"One of the clearest lessons is that the operating environment is often more complex than it initially appears.

"The busiest day of the year, rather than an average day, can reveal what a transport system really needs to deliver. Route conditions, gradients, weather, accessibility, charging opportunities and maintenance support can all influence the correct solution.

“We are also seeing greater interest in flexible layouts and fleet-management technology, as operators want better visibility of how their vehicles are being used. These conversations reinforce the importance of listening before proposing a product.”

​Making the business case


While sustainability targets may prompt fleet electrification, operators also need a clear commercial case for investing in electric vehicles. That means looking beyond the purchase price to total cost of ownership, including energy, servicing, downtime and residual value.

"The strongest business case is often found in vehicles completing frequent, predictable journeys and returning regularly to a central base," explains Lamb. "This makes charging easier to plan and allows operators to make full use of the vehicle throughout its working life.”

Beyond reducing tailpipe emissions, electric vehicles can offer lower energy costs, reduced routine maintenance and quieter operation. Quieter operation is particularly valuable in visitor areas, around animals and near hotels or accommodation.


The business case should therefore consider the vehicle's full operating life, including purchase cost, energy, servicing, downtime and residual value.

"Space is extremely valuable at most attractions," says Lamb.

"Routes may be narrow, shared with pedestrians or constrained by existing buildings, landscaping and historic infrastructure. A compact EV can negotiate tighter spaces, require less parking and operate with less disruption than a conventional road vehicle.

“This is particularly useful at heritage sites, gardens and established attractions where routes cannot easily be widened or altered.

​Towards more connected fleets


As attractions move towards lower-emission operations, site fleets are likely to become more electric, connected and tailored to specific tasks.

Rather than relying on one vehicle type, operators can combine compact passenger vehicles, utility vehicles, shuttles, and larger transport systems to meet the needs of different routes and tasks.

Lamb expects this shift to accelerate over the next five to 10 years, with data and smart technology playing a growing role.

"Attraction fleets will become increasingly electric, connected and task-specific. Rather than using one type of vehicle for every purpose, operators will build integrated fleets in which compact passenger vehicles, utility platforms, shuttles and larger transport systems each perform the work for which they are best suited.

“We are also likely to see greater use of fleet data, smarter charging and more emphasis on accessibility, whole-life costs and service support. The transition will not happen at the same speed everywhere, but the overall direction is clear."


Fleet-management systems and telematics can give operators greater visibility into vehicle location, battery performance, and maintenance needs, while smarter charging can help them manage energy use and costs.

The expansion of electric vehicles reflects a broader shift in how attractions approach site mobility. Electric vehicles can increasingly support both guest-facing transport and the back-of-house operations that keep attractions running.

For operators, the challenge is likely to be less about choosing between electric and conventional vehicles and more about determining where different types of electric vehicles can deliver the greatest operational value.

As fleets become more specialised, the emphasis will be on matching vehicles to the realities of each site, from guest transport and accessibility to maintenance, logistics and other back-of-house needs.

"Severn Lamb wants to be a long-term mobility partner within that transition, combining our established experience in passenger transport with a much broader electric vehicle portfolio,” concludes Lamb.

“Our aim is to help operators select the right solution for every part of their site, from behind-the-scenes operations to the guest journey."

Meet the Severn Lamb team in London at IAAPA Expo Europe 2026 from 22 – 24 September at booth #S1416 and in Orlando at IAAPA Expo 2026 from 17 – 20 November at booth #S3728 and #S3832.

title: Martin & Vleminckx to bring next-gen thrill attractions to IAAPA Expo Europe 2026
summary:
Martin & Vleminckx (MV Rides), a leader in the design, manufacturing, fabrication, and installation of attractions, will be exhibiting at IAAPA Expo Europe 2026, where it will present its portfolio of attractions designed to deliver unforgettable experiences, maximise operational value, and push the boundaries of ride engineering.

The expo is taking place in London from 21 - 25 September, with the trade show floor open from 22 - 24 September. Attendees can find Martin & Vleminckx at booth #S4501, to discover how the company is helping shape the future of amusement attractions.

Creating lasting value

As amusement parks continue to seek innovative ways to engage visitors and differentiate their offerings, the company's booth will highlight the G-Storm.

This unique thrill ride swings guests back and forth in a giant gondola as it travels along an elevated track, combining towering height, dynamic motion and breathtaking visuals.

The G-Storm is accompanied by the Unicoaster 2.0, which marks a new generation of interactive coaster technology.

With patented rotating seats over a roller coaster track, this attraction enables riders to control the intensity of their experience. The result is a highly repeatable attraction that offers visitors a new experience with each ride.

Also featured is the Polercoaster, a roller coaster that continues to present new possibilities within compact park footprints.

Its combination of vertical coaster elements with an exceptionally efficient layout enables owners and operators to provide top-tier thrill experiences while optimising valuable space.

Nathan Jones, president of Martin & Vleminckx, says: "Today's guests are looking for distinct ride experiences that create lasting memories.

"At Martin & Vleminckx, we are focused on helping our clients create those memorable moments through innovative attractions that combine excitement, creativity, and operational efficiency."

With decades of experience, Martin & Vleminckx has built a reputation as a trusted partner to parks worldwide. Its portfolio reflects its ongoing dedication to developing attractions that drive attendance, enhance guest satisfaction, and create lasting value for operators.

Delegates at IAAPA Expo Europe 2026 are invited to meet with the Martin & Vleminckx team to learn more about the company's attraction portfolio, discuss upcoming projects, and explore new opportunities for innovation in the attractions industry.

To schedule a meeting during the show, please email info@mvrides.com

Martin & Vleminckx recently exhibited at IAAPA Expo Asia 2026, which was held in Hong Kong from 10 - 12 June.

title: Universal reveals first 23 companies appointed to deliver UK theme park
summary:
Universal has revealed the first contractors and consultants appointed to help deliver its upcoming UK theme park and resort in Bedfordshire.

Scheduled to open in 2031, Universal United Kingdom Resort will include a theme park with several immersive lands, a 500-room hotel, and a retail, dining, and entertainment complex.

In an update shared on the Universal UK project page, Universal Destinations & Experiences said enabling works are underway.

Universal UK to open in 2031

Bovis, Galliford Try, Buro Happold, Gensler Europe, Sir Robert McAlpine and Mott MacDonald are among 23 companies appointed to support delivery of the UK resort.

Also named in the update are Wates, Winvic, Mace Consult, Arcadis, Blumano, Oxford Archaeology, Brindle & Green, and AtkinsRéalis.

The full list is as follows:

  • Wilson James Ltd
  • Winvic Construction Ltd

Universal comes to the UK: what could influence the IP we see at the new park? Universal

Universal said opportunities for regional and UK businesses will continue to grow, with the project expected to create 28,000 jobs between construction and employment, and generate £50 billion of economic benefit.

Comcast NBCUniversal is investing more than £5bn in the resort, with an additional £1bn over its first 10 years of operation.

The development will be supported by £1.3bn in government funding for local infrastructure and transport improvements.

Late last month, the UK government met with regional leaders to discuss how they can work together to maximise the benefits of the new Universal resort.

title: TicketSpice shares how smarter targeting & timing can drive attraction ticket sales
summary:
TicketSpice, an end-to-end online and on-site ticketing platform, has shared insights into what attraction marketers can learn from campaigns driving 18x return on ad spend (ROAS) and six-figure revenue.

Attraction marketing is increasingly focused on performance. Operators face rising pressure to identify which audiences are converting, which channels are effective, and where marketing investments translate into ticket sales.

That makes real campaign results especially valuable. Across recent attraction campaigns, TicketSpice has identified a few clear patterns emerging around audience targeting: timing, follow-up, and measurement.

As TicketSpice expands its marketing capabilities across email, drip campaigns, SMS and AI-assisted advertising, these patterns are becoming easier to identify and act on.

Audience targeting can significantly improve the effectiveness of paid campaigns. Paid advertising lets attractions reach potential guests outside their local area, and targeting specific audiences can improve campaign results.

Audience targeting

A motorsports venue tested four Facebook campaigns with varied interest, demographic targeting, lookalike audiences, geographic focus, and video creatives. The team spent around $4,200 on ads, resulting in nearly $64,000 in tracked ticket sales.

Each campaign achieved a ROAS ranging from 13x to 18.3x, with the top campaign targeting relevant interests and demographics within a four-hour radius of the venue.

Ad campaign performance metrics summary

These findings offer valuable insights for attraction marketers: geography alone isn't enough for targeting. Even within the same driving distance, potential buyers can vary widely in their interests, previous behaviours, and familiarity with the attraction.

To understand this better, operators should test one significant variable at a time, such as comparing a lookalike audience of past buyers with an interest-based group, experimenting with different drive radii, or using the same messaging with varied creative assets.

Proper attribution then reveals which audience and creative mix directly led to ticket sales, offering more actionable insights than click counts alone.

Those results also demonstrate the value of TicketSpice’s new AI Ad Manager. It helps attraction teams build and launch ad campaigns faster, making it easier to test different audiences and creatives, compare performance, and allocate more budget to the campaigns that are actually driving ticket sales.

Focused email campaigns

Email remains a valuable channel for attractions because it reaches past buyers and those who have already shown interest. Recent results also highlight the value of compact campaigns built around the right moment.

For a seasonal attraction, TicketSpice worked with a customer on a two-email campaign promoting a fall experience. The campaign generated 6,494 attributed ticket sales and more than $138,000 in revenue, with a 2.44% email-attributed ticket conversion rate.

A different operator ran a three-email series to promote a bull riding experience, resulting in 986 ticket sales attributed to the campaign and $17,330 in revenue, with a 2.37% conversion rate.

Another four-email series drove 3,494 attributed ticket sales and $139,860 in revenue, achieving a 6.87% ticket conversion rate from email.

Throughout these campaigns, timing and relevance proved crucial. Seasonal attractions inherently have key decision points, such as opening weekends, limited dates, pricing adjustments, holiday seasons, and nearing capacity.

TicketSpice’s email drip campaigns can target these moments with planned follow-ups, keeping the attraction top of mind as guests' visit date approaches.

Email campaign results from a TicketSpice drip campaign

Performance metrics also help teams improve future campaigns by identifying which emails generated the most sales, how quickly recipients purchased, and whether buying activity increased as the visit date approached.

These insights can inform more effective sequences for upcoming seasons.

Connecting channels

Most guests go through multiple touchpoints before making a purchase. They might see a paid ad, visit the ticket page, leave to coordinate plans, and then return after receiving an email or text reminder.

This highlights the growing importance of the relationship between channels, notes TicketSpice.

Advertising helps reach new audiences, email nurtures interest and encourages previous guests to return, and SMS messages can generate immediate urgency for limited dates, weather updates, or when capacity is nearly full.

By integrating these tools into the ticket purchase process, TicketSpice gives attraction teams a better understanding of how each touchpoint affects revenue.

Additionally, TicketSpice’s customer marketing team collaborates directly with operators to translate these features into actionable campaigns, including enhancing audience targeting, planning communications, and evaluating results.

For attractions with shorter selling seasons, that visibility can help teams make stronger marketing decisions while they still have time to influence results.

What attraction marketers can take from the results

Across these campaigns, a few patterns stand out, according ot the TicketSpice team.

First, utilise existing customer data; past ticket buyers can inform the development of more effective email audiences, lookalike audiences, and future targeting strategies.

It's also important to segment the audience with purpose, considering factors such as geography, interests, demographics, or lookalike groups, as these can perform very differently, especially for attractions that draw visitors from a wider area.

Timing plays a crucial role, so build campaigns around key moments—like upcoming dates, limited availability, or opening weekends—using email drip campaigns and SMS to keep attractions relevant. Finally, measure efforts through to the ticket sale by tracking revenue, conversion rates, and ROAS to identify which campaigns genuinely contribute to business results.

Strong campaign data gives attraction teams a better foundation for the upcoming season. It helps enhance targeting, optimise timing, refine messaging, and identify where marketing spend can be most effective.

As TicketSpice expands its marketing toolkit, the aim is to help operators turn campaign results into more transparent, actionable decisions. For many attractions, the next growth opportunity may already lie in last season’s ticketing data.

title: ​Next-gen LBE VR: inside Hololabs Studio’s new attraction format
summary:
Combining the immersion of VR with the physicality of themed environments is an ongoing challenge for location-based entertainment (LBE) operators. The challenge isn't just creating an immersive experience but delivering it at a scale and throughput that works commercially.

Hololabs Studio believes it has developed a way to address that challenge. At this year’s IAAPA Expo Europe in London, the Canadian creative technology studio is introducing a ticketed, guided, multi-room experience that combines physical sets with mixed reality.

The studio brings experience across game development, LBVR and major theme park attractions, including Mario Kart: Koopa’s Challenge at Universal Studios Japan, and Mario Kart: Bowser’s Challenge at Universal Studios in Hollywood and Orlando.

The new format is designed to tackle what Hololabs Studio describes as the “three-cornered problem” of location-based entertainment: balancing immersion, capacity, and an attraction's physical footprint.

Hololabs Studio president Mike Wozniewski and VP of creative Brett Gaylor speak to blooloop about the thinking behind the format, the company’s experience in large-scale attractions and the development of its approach to immersive entertainment.

​A new attraction format


At the core of Hololabs Studio’s new offering is a flexible, walk-through attraction format. Rather than being a single, fixed game, the format is a modular framework designed to accommodate different intellectual properties and thematic skins.

The attraction is designed as a ticketed, guided experience that moves groups of guests through three distinct rooms, each representing a different phase of the narrative and physical journey.

The demonstration skin being brought to London, called Abyss MR, is based on Abyss: Vault, Hololabs Studio's cooperative science-fiction VR experience for two to six players. Guests begin their adventure by walking into a themed, physical show set, styled as the interior of a submarine.


Inside, guests can touch and interact with physical props and controls. "One of the items in the submarine is a VR headset, themed to belong in the world, and guests are instructed to put it on before continuing through the rest of the attraction," explains Wozniewski.

Through the headset's pass-through cameras, the real and the virtual are combined. While the physical walls of the room provide structure, the headset “fills in” the details, rendering the exterior of the submarine, virtual steam rising from physical vents, and a real-time ocean outside a submarine window.

While the experience at IAAPA Expo Europe will demonstrate this first space, the eventual format will see guests move from this room, once they are oriented and the narrative is established, to a second room, an open space dedicated to free-roam VR.

The moment they cross the threshold, the pass-through camera deactivates, moving the players into an immersive digital environment where they see full-body virtual avatars of themselves and their companions.

In this room, Hololabs Studio's game design elements shine. Because they are in a completely virtual space, they are no longer restricted by the room’s physical boundaries. Through clever spatial design, guests can traverse large digital environments, scale vertical ladders, or slide down zip lines.


The experience culminates in a third room designed to deliver a cinematic climax while physically positioning the guests for exit and headset removal.

"It concludes with a seated finale and a motion base, and then they can take their headsets off. That final room can also be themed, where the seats are in an escape pod, for example," Wozniewski adds.

Operating essentially like a compact 4D cinema, the finale room uses motion, vibration and synchronised media to provide a physical conclusion before guests exit into a themed retail or food and beverage space.

Rather than waiting for a group to complete the entire experience before sending in the next, Hololabs Studio uses a "stacking" flow.

"Every guest would go into [the mixed reality space], and then they alternate into virtual reality spaces to optimise for throughput," Gaylor explains.

​Balancing immersion, capacity and footprint


The multi-room format has been developed around what Hololabs Studio describes as the “three-cornered problem” of location-based entertainment.

Operators must balance three competing requirements: high throughput, a small physical footprint, and a high degree of immersion and interactivity, to keep people coming back for more.

Achieving all three is a challenge. For example, a traditional free-roam VR arena can offer high immersion within a relatively small footprint. Still, its throughput is limited by the number of players that can occupy the space at once.

Conversely, a high-throughput dark ride can accommodate large numbers of guests but may require a significantly larger physical footprint and typically offers less individual guest agency.


"Everyone's battling with this," Wozniewski says. "We think we have a solution that elegantly accommodates all three.”

The studio has combined its game-design expertise with theme park operational logic. By dividing the guest experience into a sequence of rooms, Hololabs Studio aims to stack groups of players, increasing throughput while using a compact physical footprint and incorporating mixed-reality elements.

"This is a format that we've tuned, and we've modelled. We have calculations of the revenue per square metre, and the return on investment that someone could see if they are an operator or someone with an IP that wants to create something like this.”


The standard layout is designed for retail environments, entertainment centres or as an anchor within a larger park development. Hololabs Studio says its guest flow allows the format to accommodate a high throughput within a compact footprint.

​From game development to theme parks


Hololabs Studio has spent the past 15 years working at the intersection of gaming, software engineering and location-based entertainment.

The Canadian creative technology studio brings together former AAA game developers and systems integration specialists, with experience on projects including Universal's Mario Kart rides.

Over time, the studio has evolved from digital game design into physical-world installations that connect software with show sets, ride systems, projection, audio, lighting, and practical effects.

"A lot of us come from game development," says Wozniewski. "There's a lot of former AAA game developers at the company, and then we got into theme park development at a pretty high level, working on Mario Kart for Universal Studios."

That project helped the team to understand the operational demands of world-class attractions.

Hololabs Studio contributed gameplay, interactive media, and key elements of the technical architecture, helping to realise a ride that blended physical dark ride vehicles with augmented reality headsets, projection mapping, and real-time interactive elements.


Working on an e-ticket attraction of this scale presented Hololabs Studio with technical challenges around integrating game technology into a major theme park attraction:

"That was a perfect attraction for us to work on because Mario Kart is a video game, and we just dove right in and worked on the gameplay.

"We helped everyone figure out how to bring in game-ready assets because traditionally, theme parks work with pre-rendered media that is very heavy, and a different approach was needed for assets that could react in real time.”

"We've learned a lot over the years about how to integrate into big theme park projects," Wozniewski adds.

"There are dozens of vendors doing disparate things, and a normal game development company might not know how to incorporate triggers for special effects or embed practical effects, lighting and audio in the show sets, how to incorporate that all into one cohesive experience that's shared between multiple people and rooms.”

"We're seeing more story-driven VR experiences now that eschew pure gaming to reach broader audiences. People who grew up with video games expect certain levels of interactivity in their experiences now," says Bob Cooney, a leading consultant in location-based entertainment and VR.

"Hololab's experience designing high-throughput gamified attractions puts them in a unique position to blend deeply immersive environments with game mechanics that drive repeat visitation."


Hololabs Studio's experience gives a broad understanding of how digital technology can work alongside physical environments. Its projects have included mobile and augmented reality experiences designed to enhance physical models, as well as permanent and touring museum exhibitions such as The Education of Ursula and JellyBloom.

Across these projects, the company has focused on integrating technology into the wider visitor experience, rather than treating it as an attraction in its own right. This approach also informs Hololabs Studio's thinking about immersive technology in location-based entertainment.

​Lessons from LBVR


Hololabs Studio began applying its video game development experience to the growing location-based virtual reality (LBVR) market.

The company saw parallels between the social nature of LBE and the group experience of visiting a theme park, leading it to develop Abyss: Vault, a cooperative science-fiction adventure for two to six players on compact free-roam platforms.

"As game developers, we've made games for consoles like Xbox and PlayStation," Wozniewski says. "But finally, we found this free-roam VR category where you can make a game for a group of friends or family, and it's physical. They go to a location.

"It felt very close to that theme park vibe, and so we really enjoyed making Abyss: Vault.”


As Abyss: Vault was deployed on platforms including Spawnpoint, SynthesisVR and Vex in Europe, North America, and Asia, the team also gained a closer view of some of the practical constraints facing LBVR.

Hardware has historically presented operators with a choice between high-end systems that require more equipment and standalone headsets with more limited processing power.

Gaylor points to the impact this can have on both the operation and the visitor experience:

"Previously, virtual reality has had some headwinds in the market and with operators because either you have to have these bulky sets of equipment for the resolution to be high enough to stream from gaming PCs.

“Or, it's been on standalone headsets which have the same sort of processing power as a phone, and so the quality of the graphics is quite low, the performance of the devices can have a lower frame rate, and so that can lead to things like motion sickness.”

The team also identified a creative challenge. While theme parks have long used physical environments to shape a visitor's journey and support storytelling, Wozniewski says some LBVR experiences have placed greater emphasis on straightforward combat mechanics.


"A lot of them, you put on your headsets and basically just stand back-to-back shooting hordes of zombies that are coming at you. And so, interactivity has been there, but maybe it hasn't been done in the best way," Wozniewski says.

For Hololabs Studio, this raised a broader question about who LBVR experiences are designed for. Wozniewski argues that the audience for location-based entertainment is broader than the traditional gaming demographic.

"It's actually lots of families and diverse groups of friends going out, and so we're really trying to make experiences that resonate with all audiences.”

​New hardware, new possibilities


Hololabs says recent advances in headset hardware have helped make this type of multi-room format possible. For the new format, the studio has partnered with Pico and has developed the experience for the upcoming standalone headset, Space Pro.

"We were excited to work with the Hololabs team because they were already looking to pushing the Mixed Reality boundaries of our current hardware," says Sean Robinson, Director of Enterprise Sales & Channel, NA, PICO XR.

"We knew they were the right creators to take an unreleased product and build a novel spatial experience that exploits all of its capabilities and performance."

"What we need for the mixed reality is high-resolution pass-through," Gaylor notes, "so that when the guest is looking at the physical set, they're seeing it at a resolution where marrying the virtual onto it won't feel jarring, so that it actually feels completely mixed.”


"The newest VR headsets featuring full colour passthrough video of the real world, aka mixed reality, are enabling an entirely new class of experiences. The blending of the real and virtual really fools the mind into thinking it's all real," says Cooney.

"Because you can see the other people you're in the experience with, these experiences are inherently more social. It also eliminates any potential motion sickness, which in a high volume environment is critical."

The new class of standalone headsets provides this ultra-high-resolution pass-through camera, coupled with massive on-board processing power that eliminates the need for streaming or tethers.

“All the processing is happening on the device rather than being streamed. That allows the guests to be able to have that free-roaming experience" says Gaylor.

This on-board processing is important to the format's operation, allowing guests to move freely without a tethered system.

Rendering real-time environments directly on the headset can also reduce reliance on streamed content and minimise latency, an important consideration for VR comfort. For operators, the approach removes the need for backpack PCs and cable tethers, potentially simplifying the operational workflow.

"The market is growing such that these kinds of formats are becoming possible and profitable, and audiences are starting to respond, and say, 'Yes, these are attractions that we find exciting.’”

​Designing for interaction


While technology provides the platform, the core focus is on the quality of the interaction itself. For the Hololabs Studio team, interactivity isn't about simple point-and-click or shooting mechanics; it is about giving guests genuine, cooperative agency that drives the narrative forward.

"Theme parks are mainly pre-rendered media; it's the same story every time," Wozniewski says. "There's an opportunity to make things much more interactive and give guests agency so that they can change the experience on the fly. That's what we're all about: how do you present a goal but offer different paths to achieving that?”

Achieving this level of interactivity within a high-throughput, timed environment is not straightforward. If a game is too complex, guests may get stuck, throwing off the schedule of the multi-room format. If it is too simple, it fails to engage.

"We had to make sure that we weren’t setting the bar too high for folks who were having that first VR experience," Gaylor says.

"So, we had to grapple with challenging research questions: how can we both make this engaging for experienced players while being accessible and not alienating for new players? It had to be intuitive in the way that you would work through the story.”


To bridge this gap, Hololabs Studio focuses on social cooperation.

"We wanted to make something where you and I both needed to interact together in a really intentional way to drive the story forward," Gaylor says.

"With Abyss: Vault, we adopted a central light mechanic. To proceed through the story, guests needed to combine their coloured lights in a specific way. You might have a blue one, I would have a red one, and together we would make a magenta sensor go off, or we would be able to attack an enemy that has a magenta sensor.

“Trying to design gameplay where collaboration is actually central to the experience is really important.”

Hololabs Studio also uses spatial and mechanical design to create a sense of scale within a constrained physical footprint.

"To have the guests move through a large space, designers have often created large spaces in the real world, within a warehouse or incredibly large square footage. We tried to take what we learned from compact spaces and show how you can make a guest feel like they are moving through a large virtual world through clever spatial design.

“For example, if a guest sends a moving platform to another player, and then that player gets on the moving platform, and then in the virtual environment controls that moving platform, they can traverse a very large space. A six-by-six metre environment can actually feel like 60 by 60 metres because they have moved quite a bit around the virtual environment.”

Interactive elements such as virtual zip lines, moving platforms and climbing ladders allow the virtual journey to extend beyond the physical dimensions of the room.

​Taking the format to IAAPA Expo Europe


At IAAPA Expo Europe in London, Hololabs Studio is bringing a physical, functional “vertical slice” of the format to the show floor.

Visitors to the booth can step inside a physical set representing part of a submarine, put on a Pico headset and experience how physical controllers, surfaces and high-resolution digital pass-through work together.

The studio is presenting the format as a platform that can be adapted for different games, brands and intellectual properties. Alongside the physical demonstration, Hololabs Studio will showcase floor plans, layout designs and financial models for the format.

The layouts also incorporate operational flow, themed retail and food and beverage, reflecting Hololabs Studio's approach to secondary spend.


The format's flexibility means it can be tailored to different brands, IPs, or local markets. While the IAAPA Expo demonstration features the studio’s own sci-fi Abyss IP, Hololabs Studio already has multiple alternative concepts in development.

"Ultimately, we want people to hire us to build such an attraction for them," Wozniewski says.

“In this space, there are opportunities for collaboration, partnerships, co-productions, co-development. We're interested in people coming to IAAPA who either have the venue or have the IP; one part of the puzzle that would make these things become a reality. We are the solution for the format, the technology, the design and the interactivity.”

The format brings together the systems integration of a major theme park attraction with the social interactivity of a real-time game engine, while reducing the physical footprint required to deliver both.

The IAAPA demonstration will show operators how the combination of physical sets, mixed reality, and free-roam VR can create a scalable, commercially focused location-based entertainment format.

Meet the Hololabs Studio team at IAAPA Expo Europe at booth #N4515. The trade show floor is open from 22 to 24 September at the ExCeL London. Meetings can be booked in advance here.
